title: DevOps burden matrix — self-hosted vs managed inference
content:
Purpose: working brief for GTM and AE squads to quickly reason about customer tradeoffs when they ask about self-hosting (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM stacks). This is meant to be practical — short diagnostics, core objections + counters, and a simple per-persona decision matrix that sales/SEs can use in early discovery.

Executive thesis:
- The buyer decision rarely hinges only on peak latency or best single-request throughput. It is dominated by total operational burden (people + time), risk (security/SLAs/compliance), and the cost of maintaining parity with model innovations.
- Self-hosted stacks (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM) can win on single-case economics for very large, stable, latency-tolerant workloads where the customer already has mature infra teams and strict on-prem/regulatory needs.
- Managed platforms (Redwood) win when teams prioritize time-to-production, predictable unit economics, unified rollout tools, and peace-of-mind around SLOs, model regressions, and fallbacks.

Comparison dimensions (short):
- Performance (latency and throughput): vLLM/TGI/TensorRT can be highly optimized for specific models/hardware. TensorRT-LLM shines on NVIDIA on-prem with INT8/FP16 kernels. But chasing incremental latency gains requires continuing engineering effort. Redwood provides predictable profiles across common models and automated kernel/config suggestions.
- Cost (TCO): raw GPU-cycles alone sometimes favor self-hosting once sustained utilization > ~70% on dedicated clusters. However, include SRE/infra engineering, model conversion/debugging, monitoring, and spares — the fully loaded cost often flips in favor of managed.
- Operational burden: patching, driver & CUDA upgrades, quantization regressions, perf regressions after model updates, rolling restarts, capacity planning, telemetry instrumentation, security audits. Self-hosted stacks require senior infra/ML infra engineers.
- Model lifecycle and rollouts: Redwood has built-in canary/A-B rollouts, auto-fallbacks and version pinning. Open-source stacks require bespoke rollout infra or risky manual cutovers.
- Reliability & fallbacks: managed platforms typically offer multi-region fallback, cross-model fallback strategies, and SLA contracts. Self-hosted clusters are single-customer but fragile to capacity spikes unless engineered for bursts.
- Observability & debugging: vLLM/TGI provide logs and some telemetry, but need additional tracing and token-level cost tooling to answer product questions. Redwood instrumented-by-default telemetry reduces MTTR for regressions and quality alerts.
- Security & compliance: on-prem/VPC self-hosted is essential for some customers. Redwood Private offering closes much of this gap with customer-controlled VPC and KMS/HSM integrations.

Persona-based decision matrix (quick heuristics sales can use):
- Startup product lead building a new feature: lean team, needs speed. Recommendation: Redwood hosted API. Objections: cost. Counter: faster time-to-value, fewer engineering months spent on infra, predictable per-token pricing, free credits to validate.
- ML platform team at mid-market SaaS: already managing clusters, cares about cost efficiency and full control. Recommendation: Consider Dedicated/Private from Redwood or self-hosted for long-term cost optimization. Key question: do you have SRE + 2 ML infra engineers committed for 12+ months? If not, move to Redwood Dedicated.
- Regulated enterprise (healthcare/finance): needs strict data control and audit trail. Recommendation: Redwood Private or on-prem self-hosted if air-gapped required. Evaluate compliance gaps and ask about KMS/HSM, audit log retention and SOC/Ops runbooks.

Core objections we hear and scripted counters:
- "We can save money by running our own clusters." -> Counter: show quick TCO model. Include not just GPUs but 0.2-0.5 FTE of ML infra + 0.5-1.0 FTE SRE per team, ongoing engineering time for model conversions and perf tuning, and risk premium for outages. Use our standard TCO slide (see linked artifacts).
- "Open-source stacks innovate faster; we don't want vendor lock-in." -> Counter: Redwood supports pinned model versions, exportable prompts/evals, and private deployment options. Position Redwood as enabling portability while removing operational burden. Make portability a handshake: customers can export model artifacts and prompts but keep runtime ops to us.
- "We need absolute lowest latency for large context models." -> Counter: If they control hardware and can sustain the engineering effort to keep optimized kernels up to date, self-hosted may be best. But ask: what is your willingness to staff an engineer to chase model X regressions every quarter? Offer Redwood Dedicated or Private as hybrid approach.

Quick TCO heuristic (for discovery calls):
- Inputs we ask for: average tokens/day, peak concurrent sessions, acceptable p95 latency, current or target model(s), existing infra FTEs, compliance needs.
- Rule-of-thumb: if sustained GPU utilization > 60–70% and you have 2+ dedicated infra FTEs maintaining the stack, self-hosting starts to make sense. Otherwise, managed is cheaper when factoring people/time.

Redwood-specific positioning bullets for pitch decks / discovery emails:
- "Ship features, not infra: get consistent SLA-backed inference and built-in rollout/rollback tooling so PMs can iterate on prompt/quality without needing a full ops project."
- "Pay for running inference, not for reinventing it: we optimize kernels and batching across models, and maintain fallbacks so you don't need a cluster of experts on-call 24/7."
- "Private-first: if you need VPC or on-prem, we can run full control plane privately with KMS and audit logs — no prolonged re-architecture needed."

Checklist for AE/SE to qualify a 'self-host candidate':
1) Do they have a committed infra org (names/FTEs) that can be responsible for inference?
2) Can they tolerate 2–4 weeks of model-conversion/perf tuning for each major model change?
3) Do they require air-gapped processing or strict legal residency?
4) Are their latency targets below what managed instances provide and do they have hardware that matches benchmarking?
5) Are they willing to own rollout and observability and compensate for SRE time?

Suggested follow-ups / resources to send after a call:
- Lightweight TCO spreadsheet tailored to their tokens/day and peak concurrency (template link: CONFLUENCE-1234).
- Short demo script: show Redwood fallback in action (failover from LLM-large to LLM-small without app error), canary rollout, and token-level cost dashboard.
- If they insist on self-hosting: offer a hybrid migration plan (start on Redwood hosted, migrate to Dedicated/Private after N months once utilization/commit confirmed).

Open questions for product to answer (input needed from infra/product teams):
- Can we codify a standard TCO calculator that includes people-time multipliers for ML infra and SRE?
- What are the exact SLA+SLO tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private (we need clear language for contracts)?
- Can we create an internal benchmark pack comparing 4 representative models across vLLM/TGI/TensorRT vs Redwood for common cloud GPU types (A10G/A100/H100) to use in deals?

Notes to self / follow-ups: add a short one-pager that sales can hand to customers: single-page matrix with persona on rows and recommended path on columns. Also produce a short script for handling "I want to self-host to avoid vendor lock-in" that emphasizes portability without operational burden.

Appendix (short raw notes from recent deals):
- Deal A (late 2024): Customer had 3 infra FTEs but no ML infra experience. Initially optimistic about self-hosting, but after a 6-week POC saw perf regressions on newer LLM weights and moved to Redwood Dedicated.
- Deal B (2024): Large fintech with strict residency requirements (on-prem for some workloads). Chose a hybrid: Redwood Private for regulated routes, Redwood hosted for non-sensitive endpoints.
- Deal C (2024): Gaming company with predictable, extremely high GPU utilization (constant inference for many NPCs). Built internal stack using TensorRT-LLM and maintained 3 full-time on-call infra engineers. Net TCO favored self-hosted after year 2.

End of brief. Action items: turn this into a 1-page cheat sheet, create a 10-minute AE training video, and request benchmark results from E2E infra team.
